data.name: Cognition
data.description: Learning, memory and related brain function. mTOR inhibition can enhance cognition in young mice and blunt age-related cognitive decline.
data.description_beginner: Learning, memory, and related brain function. Turning mTOR down can sharpen thinking in young mice and may soften age-related mental decline, though the same drugs also carry real risks for brain-cell signaling.

studies.title: Chronic inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin by rapamycin modulates cognitive and non-cognitive components of behavior throughout lifespan in mice.
studies.authors: Halloran J; Hussong SA; Burbank R; Podlutskaya N; Fischer KE; Sloane LB; Austad SN; Strong R; Richardson A; Hart MJ; Galvan V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Asked whether the lifespan-extending dose of rapamycin harms or helps the aging BRAIN. Reassuringly, it enhanced learning and memory in young mice, prevented age-related cognitive decline in old ones, and even reduced anxiety and depression-like behavior - linked to boosted brain monoamines. Cognitive benefit, not cost.

studies.title: High-concentration hydrogen mitigates cognitive impairment in a murine model of Sepsis-associated encephalopathy by enhancing oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination in the mPFC
studies.authors: Yu J; Qi W; Li F; Chang B; Wang Zengkun; Kan Y; Yu Yonghao; Yu Yang
studies.journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: In a mouse model of sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE), mTOR hyperactivation impairs oligodendrocyte maturation and causes cognitive deficits; hydrogen gas and rapamycin suppress mTOR, restore myelination, and improve cognition in these mice.

studies.title: mTORC2 controls actin polymerization required for consolidation of long-term memory
studies.authors: Huang W; Zhu PJ; Zhang S; Zhou H; Stoica L; Galiano M; Krnjevic K; Roman G; Costa-Mattioli M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Conditional Rictor-knockout mice (postnatal forebrain) and Drosophila
studies.finding: Conditional deletion of Rictor in the postnatal mouse forebrain reduced mTORC2 activity and selectively impaired long-term memory and the late phase of hippocampal LTP, with a comparable long-term-memory deficit in dTORC2-deficient flies. Hippocampal actin polymerisation was reduced, and restoring it rescued both L-LTP and long-term memory; a compound that raised mTORC2 activity converted early LTP into late LTP and enhanced memory. This is the loss-of-function AND rescue evidence that mTORC2 is required for memory consolidation - the arm chronic rapamycin also disrupts, and the study Open Question H8 needs for its mTORC2 liability leg, which until 2026-09-05 rested on no supporting study at all.

studies.title: Aberrant excitatory neuronal ERBB4 promotes Alzheimer's disease pathology
studies.authors: Lee SY; Park E; Lee HE; Kim S; Yeo Y; Park J; Choi YJ; Lee K; Yoon KJ; Park S; Kim E; Kim JI; Chung WS

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse AD models (5xFAD/APP), excitatory-neuron-specific Erbb4 deletion and overexpression; human AD single-nucleus transcriptomics
studies.finding: Ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons is one of the earliest changes in AD mouse models and is necessary for synapse loss, reactive gliosis, amyloid plaque deposition and cognitive deficits in AD mice, and its overexpression in wild-type excitatory neurons is sufficient to reproduce synapse loss, gliosis and cognitive deficits (but not amyloid plaques); these effects require mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

studies.title: Lifelong rapamycin administration ameliorates age-dependent cognitive deficits by reducing IL-1β and enhancing NMDA signaling
studies.authors: Majumder S; Caccamo A; Medina DX; Benavides AD; Javors MA; Kraig E; Strong R; Richardson A; Oddo S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: C57BL6/129svj mice (n=20 per group): encapsulated rapamycin in food (14 mg/kg food) from 2 to 18 months, from 15 to 18 months, or control diet; Morris water maze; brain cytokines, p-S6K, NR2B and CREB phosphorylation
studies.finding: Mice were fed rapamycin in their food either from 2 months of age or only from 15 months, when age-related memory deficits were already present, and all were tested at 18 months in a water maze (20 mice per group). Mice treated from 2 months learned the hidden-platform location faster and spent more time in the target quadrant in the memory test (28.7 vs 21.3 seconds for controls), while mice started at 15 months did no better than controls. Both rapamycin groups had lower phosphorylation of S6K in the brain, a marker of mTOR activity. The improvement in the early-treated mice went together with lower IL-1beta in brain and hippocampus and higher phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B and of CREB, which the authors propose as the route. Boundary: Mice of one mixed strain, normal ageing (not an Alzheimer model); the late-start arm showed no reversal of existing deficits, and the IL-1beta and NMDA links are correlations, not tested by blocking them.

studies.title: Translational control of long-lasting synaptic plasticity and memory
studies.authors: Costa-Mattioli M; Sossin WS; Klann E; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Narrative review (no new data): genetic, physiological, pharmacological and biochemical studies in rodents, Aplysia and Drosophila
studies.finding: This review gathers evidence that long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory depend on new protein synthesis, and that the step where mRNA translation starts is a main control point. It covers two arms: the mTORC1 arm (4E-BP2, eIF4E, S6K) that controls cap-dependent translation, and the eIF2alpha arm (GCN2, PKR, ATF4) that controls general translation and specific mRNAs. It also discusses how faulty translational control is linked to disorders such as fragile X syndrome and tuberous sclerosis. It is a summary of work by many labs and gives the field a shared framework rather than new data. Boundary: narrative review; the cited evidence is mainly from rodent slices, rodent behaviour and invertebrate models, not from people.
